claim: Candida albicans is a commensal fungus that colonizes the epithelial surfaces of 30–70% of healthy individuals.
source: Candida albicans is a commensal fungus that colonizes the epithelial surfaces of 30–70% of healthy individuals (Perlroth et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perlroth et al., 2007

claim: In immune-compromised individuals, C. albicans can cause invasive, life-threatening disease.
source: However, in immune-compromised individuals, C. albicans can cause invasive, life-threatening disease.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about C. albicans pathogenicity

claim: The mortality rate for infected patients is 46–75%.
source: The mortality rate for infected patients is 46–75%, with candidiasis classified as the fourth most common nosocomial bloodstream infection (Brown et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2012

claim: Candidiasis is classified as the fourth most common nosocomial bloodstream infection.
source: The mortality rate for infected patients is 46–75%, with candidiasis classified as the fourth most common nosocomial bloodstream infection (Brown et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2012

claim: Invasive candidiasis is correlated with a switch of C. albicans from its yeast form to a hyphal form.
source: Invasive candidiasis is correlated with a switch of C. albicans from its yeast form to a hyphal form, a shift that can be induced in vitro by nutrient deprivation among other cues (reviewed in Sudbery, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sudbery, 2011 review

claim: The yeast-to-hyphal switch can be induced in vitro by nutrient deprivation among other cues.
source: Invasive candidiasis is correlated with a switch of C. albicans from its yeast form to a hyphal form, a shift that can be induced in vitro by nutrient deprivation among other cues (reviewed in Sudbery, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sudbery, 2011 review

claim: C. albicans hyphae are capable of invading epithelium and endothelium.
source: In vivo, C. albicans hyphae are capable of invading epithelium and endothelium; in addition C. albicans is capable of forming recalcitrant biofilms and inducing inflammation (Sudbery, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sudbery, 2011

claim: C. albicans is capable of forming recalcitrant biofilms.
source: In vivo, C. albicans hyphae are capable of invading epithelium and endothelium; in addition C. albicans is capable of forming recalcitrant biofilms and inducing inflammation (Sudbery, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sudbery, 2011

claim: C. albicans induces inflammation.
source: In vivo, C. albicans hyphae are capable of invading epithelium and endothelium; in addition C. albicans is capable of forming recalcitrant biofilms and inducing inflammation (Sudbery, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sudbery, 2011

claim: Impairment of the phagocytic response by elimination of macrophages and neutrophils is associated with disseminated candidiasis.
source: Accordingly, impairment of the phagocytic response, e.g. by elimination of macrophages and neutrophils, is associated with disseminated candidiasis (reviewed in Netea et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Netea et al., 2015 review

claim: The C. albicans cell wall is composed mostly (80–90%) of polysaccharides.
source: The C. albicans cell wall is composed mostly (80–90%) of polysaccharides, containing ≈ 60% β-(1,3) and -(1,6) glucans, and ≈ 40% O- and N-linked mannans (Ruiz-Herrera et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruiz-Herrera et al., 2006

claim: The C. albicans cell wall contains approximately 60% β-(1,3) and -(1,6) glucans.
source: The C. albicans cell wall is composed mostly (80–90%) of polysaccharides, containing ≈ 60% β-(1,3) and -(1,6) glucans, and ≈ 40% O- and N-linked mannans (Ruiz-Herrera et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruiz-Herrera et al., 2006

claim: The C. albicans cell wall contains approximately 40% O- and N-linked mannans.
source: The C. albicans cell wall is composed mostly (80–90%) of polysaccharides, containing ≈ 60% β-(1,3) and -(1,6) glucans, and ≈ 40% O- and N-linked mannans (Ruiz-Herrera et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruiz-Herrera et al., 2006

claim: The main non-opsonic phagocytic receptors for C. albicans are the C-type lectin family of receptors, including Dectin1, the mannose receptor, and DC-SIGN.
source: As such, the main non-opsonic phagocytic receptors for C. albicans are the C-type lectin family of receptors, including Dectin1, the mannose receptor, and DC-SIGN (reviewed in Hardison and Brown, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hardison and Brown, 2012 review

claim: The hyphal form of C. albicans can grow at a rate of 18.8 μm hr−1.
source: The hyphal form of C. albicans can grow at a rate of 18.8 μm hr−1 (GOW and Gooday, 1982), quickly exceeding the size of the phagocytes themselves.
evidence: Supported by citation to GOW and Gooday, 1982

claim: C. albicans hyphae quickly exceed the size of phagocytes themselves.
source: The hyphal form of C. albicans can grow at a rate of 18.8 μm hr−1 (GOW and Gooday, 1982), quickly exceeding the size of the phagocytes themselves.
evidence: Inferred from the growth rate data and knowledge of phagocyte size

claim: Macrophages migrate to infection sites later than polymorphonuclear cells.
source: The challenge is greatest for macrophages, which migrate to infection sites later than the polymorphonuclear cells, and thus encounter growing hyphae (reviewed in Erwig and Gow, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Erwig and Gow, 2016 review

claim: Macrophages encounter growing hyphae at infection sites.
source: The challenge is greatest for macrophages, which migrate to infection sites later than the polymorphonuclear cells, and thus encounter growing hyphae (reviewed in Erwig and Gow, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Erwig and Gow, 2016 review

claim: RAW 264.7 macrophages stably expressing the Dectin1 receptor were used to optimize the phagocytosis of C. albicans.
source: To optimize the phagocytosis of C. albicans, which has a cell wall rich in β-glucans (Gow et al., 2011), we used RAW 264.7 macrophages stably expressing the Dectin1 receptor (RAW-Dectin1; Esteban et al., 2011).
evidence: Describes the experimental approach used in the study

claim: C. albicans has a cell wall rich in β-glucans.
source: To optimize the phagocytosis of C. albicans, which has a cell wall rich in β-glucans (Gow et al., 2011), we used RAW 264.7 macrophages stably expressing the Dectin1 receptor (RAW-Dectin1; Esteban et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gow et al., 2011

claim: C. albicans hyphae were considerably longer (>15 μm) than the macrophages (8–10 μm in diameter).
source: Under the conditions used to generate them, C. albicans hyphae were considerably longer (>15 μm) than the macrophages (8–10 μm in diameter).
evidence: Describes observational data from the experiments

claim: After 1 hr of co-incubation with macrophages, the yeast form was fully engulfed.
source: After 1 hr of co-incubation with the macrophages the yeast form was fully engulfed (Figure 1A), while a significant number of hyphal C. albicans were only partially internalized (68.5% ± 4.5, while 31.5% ± 4.6 were fully internalized; 1019 events from 12 independent experiments), which was verified using fluorescent concanavalin A to label exposed hyphae (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: 68.5% ± 4.5 of hyphal C. albicans were only partially internalized after 1 hr of co-incubation with macrophages.
source: After 1 hr of co-incubation with the macrophages the yeast form was fully engulfed (Figure 1A), while a significant number of hyphal C. albicans were only partially internalized (68.5% ± 4.5, while 31.5% ± 4.6 were fully internalized; 1019 events from 12 independent experiments), which was verified using fluorescent concanavalin A to label exposed hyphae (Figure 1B).
evidence: Quantitative data from 1019 events across 12 independent experiments

claim: 31.5% ± 4.6 of hyphal C. albicans were fully internalized after 1 hr of co-incubation with macrophages.
source: After 1 hr of co-incubation with the macrophages the yeast form was fully engulfed (Figure 1A), while a significant number of hyphal C. albicans were only partially internalized (68.5% ± 4.5, while 31.5% ± 4.6 were fully internalized; 1019 events from 12 independent experiments), which was verified using fluorescent concanavalin A to label exposed hyphae (Figure 1B).
evidence: Quantitative data from 1019 events across 12 independent experiments

claim: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed that most hyphae were only partially internalized.
source: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed that most hyphae were only partially internalized (Figure 1C) and, in addition, revealed the existence around the neck of the frustrated phagosome of a low-contrast structure seemingly devoid of membrane-bound organelles (Figure 1C, inset), previously interpreted by Strijbis et al., 2013 as accumulated actin.
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1C

claim: A low-contrast structure seemingly devoid of membrane-bound organelles exists around the neck of the frustrated phagosome.
source: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed that most hyphae were only partially internalized (Figure 1C) and, in addition, revealed the existence around the neck of the frustrated phagosome of a low-contrast structure seemingly devoid of membrane-bound organelles (Figure 1C, inset), previously interpreted by Strijbis et al., 2013 as accumulated actin.
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1C inset

claim: The low-contrast structure around the neck of the frustrated phagosome was previously interpreted as accumulated actin.
source: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed that most hyphae were only partially internalized (Figure 1C) and, in addition, revealed the existence around the neck of the frustrated phagosome of a low-contrast structure seemingly devoid of membrane-bound organelles (Figure 1C, inset), previously interpreted by Strijbis et al., 2013 as accumulated actin.
evidence: Supported by citation to Strijbis et al., 2013

claim: The region around the neck of the frustrated phagosome corresponds to an actin-rich cuff-like structure.
source: Indeed, this region corresponded to an actin-rich cuff-like structure (Figure 1D); F-actin was so highly accumulated at the cuff that the remainder of the cellular actin could only be visualized when images were overexposed (Figure 1D, inset).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1D

claim: F-actin is so highly accumulated at the cuff that the remainder of the cellular actin can only be visualized when images are overexposed.
source: Indeed, this region corresponded to an actin-rich cuff-like structure (Figure 1D); F-actin was so highly accumulated at the cuff that the remainder of the cellular actin could only be visualized when images were overexposed (Figure 1D, inset).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and inset

claim: The base of the frustrated phagocytic cup is virtually devoid of F-actin.
source: Note that the remainder (i.e. the base) of the frustrated phagocytic cup was virtually devoid of F-actin.
evidence: Observational data from fluorescence microscopy

claim: The actin cuff occurred in 96.3% ± 1.9 of the partially internalized hyphae.
source: This actin cuff was observed for RAW-Dectin1 cells engulfing C. albicans hyphae up to 100 μm in size (data not shown), and occurred in 96.3% ± 1.9 of the partially internalized hyphae (674 events analyzed in 12 independent experiments).
evidence: Quantitative data from 674 events across 12 independent experiments

claim: The actin cuff was observed for RAW-Dectin1 cells engulfing C. albicans hyphae up to 100 μm in size.
source: This actin cuff was observed for RAW-Dectin1 cells engulfing C. albicans hyphae up to 100 μm in size (data not shown), and occurred in 96.3% ± 1.9 of the partially internalized hyphae (674 events analyzed in 12 independent experiments).
evidence: Observational data from experiments

claim: Actin cuff-like structures have been reported during the phagocytosis of various filamentous targets.
source: These data support published accounts of actin cuff-like structures seen during the phagocytosis of various filamentous targets (García-Rodas et al., 2011; Gerisch et al., 2009; Heinsbroek et al., 2009; Prashar et al., 2013; Strijbis et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Frustrated phagocytosis with formation of a pronounced actin cuff occurs in murine primary macrophages confronted with C. albicans hyphae.
source: The occurrence of frustrated phagocytosis with formation of a pronounced actin cuff was not unique to the RAW-Dectin1 cell line; similar features were seen when murine or human primary macrophages were confronted with C. albicans hyphae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B, respectively).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Frustrated phagocytosis with formation of a pronounced actin cuff occurs in human primary macrophages confronted with C. albicans hyphae.
source: The occurrence of frustrated phagocytosis with formation of a pronounced actin cuff was not unique to the RAW-Dectin1 cell line; similar features were seen when murine or human primary macrophages were confronted with C. albicans hyphae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B, respectively).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: The actin cuff is remarkably stable, lasting for at least 90 min without contracting.
source: The actin cuff was remarkably stable, lasting for at least 90 min without contracting (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1I

claim: The actin composing the cuff undergoes measurable turnover (treadmilling).
source: Nevertheless, the actin composing these structures undergoes measurable turnover (treadmilling), since the cuffs underwent gradual disassembly when the cells were treated with latrunculin A, which scavenges actin monomers (last two panels, Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by latrunculin A treatment data shown in Figure 1I

claim: Latrunculin A scavenges actin monomers.
source: Nevertheless, the actin composing these structures undergoes measurable turnover (treadmilling), since the cuffs underwent gradual disassembly when the cells were treated with latrunculin A, which scavenges actin monomers (last two panels, Figure 1I).
evidence: Established knowledge about the mechanism of latrunculin A

claim: Dectin1 was concentrated in patches along the frustrated phagocytic cup but was poorly detectable near the actin cuff.
source: Remarkably, while Dectin1 was clearly concentrated in patches elsewhere along the frustrated phagocytic cup, it was poorly detectable by immunostaining near the actin cuff (ratio cuff: cup 0.60 ± 0.04; n = 30 p<0.0001; Figure 2A and inset).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A with quantification

claim: The ratio of Dectin1 fluorescence at the cuff compared to the cup was 0.60 ± 0.04 (n = 30, p<0.0001).
source: Remarkably, while Dectin1 was clearly concentrated in patches elsewhere along the frustrated phagocytic cup, it was poorly detectable by immunostaining near the actin cuff (ratio cuff: cup 0.60 ± 0.04; n = 30 p<0.0001; Figure 2A and inset).
evidence: Quantitative data from 30 measurements

claim: Emerald-Dectin1 showed similar distribution to immunostained Dectin1, with ratio cuff: cup 0.56 ± 0.04 (n = 15, p<0.0001).
source: The failure to detect accumulation of Dectin1 at these sites was not attributable to masking of the exofacial epitope, possibly resulting from tight apposition to the hyphae, because similar results were obtained when the receptors were tagged with emerald fluorescent protein and visualized directly in live cells (ratio cuff: cup 0.56 ± 0.04; n = 15, p<0.0001; Figure 2B and inset).
evidence: Quantitative data from 15 measurements shown in Figure 2B

claim: Host E- or N-cadherin have been reported to contribute to C. albicans internalization in epithelial and endothelial cells, respectively.
source: In epithelial and endothelial cells, host E- or N-cadherin, respectively, have been reported to contribute to C. albicans internalization (Moreno-Ruiz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moreno-Ruiz et al., 2009

claim: The cadherin-mediated internalization process involves the recruitment of α- and β-catenins and activation of the Arp2/3 pathway for actin nucleation.
source: This process involved the recruitment of α- and β-catenins and activation of the Arp2/3 pathway for actin nucleation.
evidence: Describes mechanism from prior literature

claim: E-cadherin and β-catenin accumulate at sites where C. albicans hyphae are being internalized by epithelial A431 cells, with particular accumulation at sites where actin polymerizes.
source: In agreement with these reports, we observed E-cadherin and β-catenin accumulation at sites of where C. albicans hyphae were being internalized by epithelial A431 cells, with particular accumulation at sites where actin polymerized (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Neither E-cadherin nor β-catenin was detectable in RAW-Dectin1 cells or in primary human macrophages by immunoblotting.
source: However, neither E-cadherin nor β-catenin was detectable in RAW-Dectin1 cells or in primary human macrophages by immunoblotting (Figure 2C) or by immunofluorescence (not illustrated).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2C

claim: E-cadherin-GFP expressed heterologously in macrophages lines the surface membrane but is absent from the phagocytic cup.
source: When expressed heterologously in macrophages E-cadherin-GFP was found to line the surface membrane, but was absent from the phagocytic cup (Figure 2D), while β-catenin-GFP was largely soluble and did not accumulate at the cuff (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2D

claim: β-catenin-GFP expressed heterologously in macrophages is largely soluble and does not accumulate at the cuff.
source: When expressed heterologously in macrophages E-cadherin-GFP was found to line the surface membrane, but was absent from the phagocytic cup (Figure 2D), while β-catenin-GFP was largely soluble and did not accumulate at the cuff (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2E

claim: E-cadherin and β-catenin are unlikely to mediate phagocytosis of C. albicans in macrophages.
source: Thus, E-cadherin and β-catenin are unlikely to mediate phagocytosis of C. albicans in macrophages.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of expression and localization data

claim: Omission of Ca2+ had no effect on actin cuff formation in C. albicans-infected RAW-Dectin1 cells.
source: As shown in Figure 2F, omission of Ca2+ had no effect on actin cuff formation in C. albicans-infected RAW-Dectin1 cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Canonical integrin activation and ligand binding require divalent cations.
source: However, canonical integrin activation and ligand binding require divalent cations (reviewed in Leitinger et al., 2000), and would therefore be inhibited by their chelation with EDTA.
evidence: Supported by citation to Leitinger et al., 2000 review

claim: Actin cuffs formed normally in CALDAG-GEF1−/− macrophages.
source: Moreover, actin cuffs formed normally in CALDAG-GEF1−/− macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the notion that cuff formation was independent of canonical activation of integrins, which involves Rap1 (reviewed in Hogg et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Canonical activation of integrins involves Rap1.
source: Moreover, actin cuffs formed normally in CALDAG-GEF1−/− macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the notion that cuff formation was independent of canonical activation of integrins, which involves Rap1 (reviewed in Hogg et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hogg et al., 2011 review

claim: The α chain of integrin CR3 (Mac1) contains a lectin-like domain (LLD) that binds carbohydrates in a divalent cation-independent manner.
source: The α chain of the integrin complement receptor 3 (CR3, also referred to as Mac1), is unique in that it contains a lectin-like domain (LLD) that binds carbohydrates in a divalent cation-independent manner (Thornton et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thornton et al., 1996

claim: The LLD of CR3 is separate from the I-domain, the conventional ligand-binding domain of integrins.
source: The LLD is separate from the I-domain –the conventional ligand-binding domain of integrins (reviewed in Ross, 2002)– and, interestingly, binds fungal β-glucan (Ross et al., 1985; Vetvicka et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ross, 2002 review

claim: The LLD of CR3 binds fungal β-glucan.
source: The LLD is separate from the I-domain –the conventional ligand-binding domain of integrins (reviewed in Ross, 2002)– and, interestingly, binds fungal β-glucan (Ross et al., 1985; Vetvicka et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ross et al., 1985 and Vetvicka et al., 1996

claim: Both CD11b and CD18 accumulated in the region of the actin cuff in RAW-Dectin1 cells that had partially internalized C. albicans hyphae.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3, both CD11b and CD18 accumulated in the region of the actin cuff in RAW-Dectin1 cells that had partially internalized C. albicans hyphae (CD11b ratio cuff: cup 4.75 ± 0.29; n = 30, p<0.0001; CD18 ratio cuff: cup 4.79 ± 0.28; n = 30, p<0.0001; Figure 3A,B and insets).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A and 3B with quantification

claim: The CD11b ratio cuff: cup was 4.75 ± 0.29 (n = 30, p<0.0001).
source: As illustrated in Figure 3, both CD11b and CD18 accumulated in the region of the actin cuff in RAW-Dectin1 cells that had partially internalized C. albicans hyphae (CD11b ratio cuff: cup 4.75 ± 0.29; n = 30, p<0.0001; CD18 ratio cuff: cup 4.79 ± 0.28; n = 30, p<0.0001; Figure 3A,B and insets).
evidence: Quantitative data from 30 measurements

claim: The CD18 ratio cuff: cup was 4.79 ± 0.28 (n = 30, p<0.0001).
source: As illustrated in Figure 3, both CD11b and CD18 accumulated in the region of the actin cuff in RAW-Dectin1 cells that had partially internalized C. albicans hyphae (CD11b ratio cuff: cup 4.75 ± 0.29; n = 30, p<0.0001; CD18 ratio cuff: cup 4.79 ± 0.28; n = 30, p<0.0001; Figure 3A,B and insets).
evidence: Quantitative data from 30 measurements

claim: Talin, vinculin and paxillin were localized to the cuff.
source: Moreover, talin, vinculin and paxillin were also localized to the cuff (Figure 3C,D and insets; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and inset), as was HS1, the homologue of cortactin in leukocytes (Figure 3E and inset).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: HS1, the homologue of cortactin in leukocytes, was localized to the cuff.
source: Moreover, talin, vinculin and paxillin were also localized to the cuff (Figure 3C,D and insets; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and inset), as was HS1, the homologue of cortactin in leukocytes (Figure 3E and inset).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E

claim: HS1 is thought to regulate actin nucleation and branching.
source: Like cortactin, HS1 is thought to regulate actin nucleation and branching (Daly, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Daly, 2004

claim: Engagement of CR3 at the cuff is required for the formation of the underlying actin cuff.
source: Engagement of CR3 at the cuff is required for the formation of the underlying actin cuff, a process likely mediated by talin and vinculin, which were also found accumulated at the site.
evidence: Inferred from the localization data and known functions of these proteins

claim: The entire assembly appears central to the establishment of the diffusion barrier, which is lost when blocking CR3 binding with the M1/70 antibody.
source: The entire assembly appears central to the establishment of the diffusion barrier, which is lost when blocking CR3 binding with the M1/70 antibody and also when latrunculin is used to disassemble actin filaments.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results with M1/70 antibody and latrunculin

claim: The diffusion barrier is lost when latrunculin is used to disassemble actin filaments.
source: The entire assembly appears central to the establishment of the diffusion barrier, which is lost when blocking CR3 binding with the M1/70 antibody and also when latrunculin is used to disassemble actin filaments.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results with latrunculin

claim: The LLD of CR3 is located at the membrane-proximal C terminus between residues 943–1047.
source: This LLD, located at the membrane-proximal C terminus (between residues 943–1047; Lu et al., 1998) is distinct from the traditional ligand-binding I domain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 1998

claim: The LLD can bind β-glucan while the integrin is in the inactive, bent conformation.
source: Importantly, the LLD can bind β-glucan in a Ca2+-independent manner while the integrin is in the inactive, bent conformation (Thornton et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thornton et al., 1996

claim: Binding of glucan induces a semi-active conformation of the integrin that is predicted to facilitate outside-in signaling.
source: Binding of glucan has been shown to induce a semi-active conformation of the integrin that is predicted to facilitate outside-in signaling (O'Brien et al., 2012; Vetvicka et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Brien et al., 2012 and Vetvicka et al., 1996

claim: Dectin1 is required for adhesion and the initiation of phagocytosis but does not have a direct role in actin cuff formation.
source: We found that Dectin1 did not have a direct role in actin cuff formation, being instead required for adhesion and the initiation of phagocytosis.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing Dectin1 distribution and blocking experiments

claim: When Dectin1 expression is low, the deposition of opsonins contained in serum suffices to engage CR3 and promote actin cuff formation directly.
source: Interestingly, when Dectin1 expression is low, the deposition of opsonins contained in serum –including complement and possibly also anti-Candida antibodies– suffice to engage CR3 and promote actin cuff formation directly activating this process, as predicted from earlier observations (Boxx et al., 2010; Kozel et al., 1987; Vetvicka et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Boxx et al., 2010; Kozel et al., 1987; Vetvicka et al., 1996

claim: Dectin1 signaling can initiate inside-out activation of CR3.
source: Dectin1 signaling can initiate inside-out activation of CR3 (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2011

claim: Conventional Rap1-dependent inside-out signaling mediated by CalDAG-GEF1 was dispensable for actin cuff formation.
source: However, conventional Rap1-dependent inside-out signaling mediated by CalDAG-GEF1 was dispensable for actin cuff formation, as were divalent cations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from CalDAG-GEF1 knockout experiments

claim: It is likely that CR3 binds fungal β-glucan in a manner that does not require inside-out activation by Dectin1.
source: Therefore, it is likely that CR3 binds fungal β-glucan in a manner that does not require inside-out activation by Dectin1.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing independence from CalDAG-GEF1 and divalent cations

claim: Mannan had no effect on actin cuff formation.
source: We showed that mannan, a ligand for the mannose receptor, had no effect on actin cuff formation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sugar blocking experiments

claim: The utilization of C. albicans GRACE strains confirmed that mannan was dispensable for actin cuff formation.
source: The utilization of a curated set of C. albicans GRACE strains confirmed that mannan was dispensable and further excluded chitin and β(1,6)-glucan as ligands for cuff formation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using GRACE strains shown in Figure 4C and 4D

claim: Chitin was excluded as a ligand for actin cuff formation.
source: The utilization of a curated set of C. albicans GRACE strains confirmed that mannan was dispensable and further excluded chitin and β(1,6)-glucan as ligands for cuff formation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using GRACE strains shown in Figure 4C and 4D

claim: β(1,6)-glucan was excluded as a ligand for actin cuff formation.
source: The utilization of a curated set of C. albicans GRACE strains confirmed that mannan was dispensable and further excluded chitin and β(1,6)-glucan as ligands for cuff formation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using GRACE strains shown in Figure 4C and 4D

claim: 5 ng mL−1 caspofungin reduced actin cuff formation by approximately 80%.
source: The inhibitory effect of caspofungin on actin cuff formation was dose-dependent (Figure 4F), reaching ≈ 80% at 5 ng mL−1 caspofungin, a dose that reduced the β(1,3)-glucan content of the wall by 55.3%, as assessed by aniline blue staining.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: 5 ng mL−1 caspofungin reduced the β(1,3)-glucan content of the wall by 55.3%.
source: The inhibitory effect of caspofungin on actin cuff formation was dose-dependent (Figure 4F), reaching ≈ 80% at 5 ng mL−1 caspofungin, a dose that reduced the β(1,3)-glucan content of the wall by 55.3%, as assessed by aniline blue staining.
evidence: Supported by aniline blue staining data

claim: Actin cuff formation around caspofungin-treated hyphae could not be rescued by serum opsonization.
source: Actin cuff formation around caspofungin-treated hyphae could not be rescued by serum opsonization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that β(1,3)-glucan is the ligand that promotes actin cuff assembly via CR3.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: β(1,3)-glucan is the ligand that promotes actin cuff assembly via CR3.
source: Actin cuff formation around caspofungin-treated hyphae could not be rescued by serum opsonization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that β(1,3)-glucan is the ligand that promotes actin cuff assembly via CR3.
evidence: Inferred from the caspofungin and opsonization experiments

claim: Aspergillus fumigatus hyphae were able to elicit actin cuff formation by RAW-Dectin1 cells.
source: Interestingly, Aspergillus fumigatus hyphae (routinely exceeding 80 µm in length) were also able to illicit actin cuff formation by RAW-Dectin1 cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G

claim: A. fumigatus hyphae have cell wall-associated β(1,3)-glucan.
source: A. fumigatus hyphae, while displaying some unique cell wall components compared to C. albicans hyphae, also have cell wall-associated β(1,3)-glucan (Erwig and Gow, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Erwig and Gow, 2016

claim: Ligation of fungal β(1,3)-glucan by CR3 is required for actin cuff formation during frustrated phagocytosis of long hyphae.
source: We concluded that ligation of fungal β(1,3)-glucan by CR3 is required for actin cuff formation during frustrated phagocytosis of long hyphae.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental results with caspofungin, GRACE strains, and A. fumigatus

claim: Clustered CR3 acts as an initiator of actin polymerization and a key constituent of the diffusion barrier.
source: Our observations implicate clustered CR3 as an initiator of actin polymerization and a key constituent of the diffusion barrier.
evidence: Inferred from the localization and functional data

claim: The signals mediating actin polymerization at the cuff include activation of Syk.
source: The signals mediating this effect include activation of Syk, which had been reported earlier (Strijbis et al., 2013), and also of Pyk2 and Fak.
evidence: Supported by citation to Strijbis et al., 2013 and current experimental data

claim: The signals mediating actin polymerization at the cuff include activation of Pyk2 and Fak.
source: The signals mediating this effect include activation of Syk, which had been reported earlier (Strijbis et al., 2013), and also of Pyk2 and Fak.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing phosphorylated Pyk2 and Fak at the cuff

claim: Pyk2 and Fak were enriched at the cuff.
source: The latter related kinases were enriched at the cuff and dual inhibition by PF573228 blocked cuff formation.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5C and 5D

claim: Dual inhibition of Pyk2 and Fak by PF573228 blocked cuff formation.
source: The latter related kinases were enriched at the cuff and dual inhibition by PF573228 blocked cuff formation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Syk, Pyk2 and Fak have been shown to interact with β2 integrins, including CR3.
source: Along with activated Syk, Pyk2 and Fak have been shown to interact with β2 integrins, including CR3 (Duong and Rodan, 2000; Fernandez and Suchard, 1998; Han et al., 2010; Hildebrand et al., 1995; Kamen et al., 2011; Mócsai et al., 2002; Raab et al., 2017; Rubel et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2010; Yan and Novak, 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Pyk2 is required for paxillin and Vav1 activation during integrin engagement and CR3-mediated phagocytosis.
source: Pyk2, in particular, is required for paxillin and Vav1 activation during integrin engagement and CR3-mediated phagocytosis (Kamen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kamen et al., 2011

claim: Paxillin acts as a scaffold, bridging integrin-initiated complexes with Rho-GTPases.
source: Paxillin was proposed to act as a scaffold, bridging integrin-initiated complexes with Rho-GTPases (Deakin and Turner, 2008), and Vav1, previously identified as important for the phagocytosis of C. albicans (Strijbis et al., 2013), also links β2 integrins to the activation of Cdc42, Rac1 and RhoA (Gakidis et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deakin and Turner, 2008

claim: Vav1 links β2 integrins to the activation of Cdc42, Rac1 and RhoA.
source: Paxillin was proposed to act as a scaffold, bridging integrin-initiated complexes with Rho-GTPases (Deakin and Turner, 2008), and Vav1, previously identified as important for the phagocytosis of C. albicans (Strijbis et al., 2013), also links β2 integrins to the activation of Cdc42, Rac1 and RhoA (Gakidis et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gakidis et al., 2004

claim: Paxillin and active Rac1/Cdc42 were detected at the actin cuff.
source: These signaling events appear conserved during the frustrated phagocytosis of C. albicans hyphae, as we detected paxillin and active Rac1/Cdc42 at the actin cuff, and Vav1 was found to be enriched in actin cuff-like structures around C. albicans (Strijbis et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and Figure 5F

claim: Vav1 was found to be enriched in actin cuff-like structures around C. albicans.
source: These signaling events appear conserved during the frustrated phagocytosis of C. albicans hyphae, as we detected paxillin and active Rac1/Cdc42 at the actin cuff, and Vav1 was found to be enriched in actin cuff-like structures around C. albicans (Strijbis et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Strijbis et al., 2013

claim: The actin cuffs formed around C. albicans hyphae were singularly sensitive to SM1-FH2 and therefore dependent on formin-mediated linear actin polymerization.
source: The actin cuffs formed around C. albicans hyphae were singularly sensitive to SM1-FH2 –and therefore dependent on formin-mediated linear actin polymerization– and not to inhibitors of the Arp2/3 complex that promotes branched actin polymerization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G

claim: The actin cuffs were not sensitive to inhibitors of the Arp2/3 complex.
source: The actin cuffs formed around C. albicans hyphae were singularly sensitive to SM1-FH2 –and therefore dependent on formin-mediated linear actin polymerization– and not to inhibitors of the Arp2/3 complex that promotes branched actin polymerization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G

claim: CR3 initiates signaling through Syk and Pyk2/Fak, leading to activation of Vav1 and Rho GTPases, culminating in formin-dependent actin nucleation.
source: Collectively, our findings support a model whereby CR3 initiates signaling through Syk and Pyk2/Fak, leading to activation of Vav1 and Rho GTPases, culminating in formin-dependent actin nucleation.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental results on signaling pathways

claim: PtdIns(4,5)P2 is present at the plasmalemma but is not detectable in the phagosomal membrane.
source: PtdIns(4,5)P2 is present at the plasmalemma but is not detectable in the phagosomal membrane, while PtdIns(3)P and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 co-exist in the phagosomes yet are absent from the surface membrane.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6A

claim: PtdIns(3)P and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 co-exist in the phagosomes yet are absent from the surface membrane.
source: PtdIns(4,5)P2 is present at the plasmalemma but is not detectable in the phagosomal membrane, while PtdIns(3)P and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 co-exist in the phagosomes yet are absent from the surface membrane.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6B and 6C

claim: PtdIns(4,5)P2 was present in the surface membrane facing the extracellular milieu but was undetectable in the invaginated section that constituted the frustrated phagosome.
source: Remarkably, while PtdIns(4,5)P2 was present as expected in the surface membrane facing the extracellular milieu, it was undetectable in the invaginated section that constituted the frustrated phagosome (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by PLCδ-PH-GFP biosensor data shown in Figure 6A

claim: PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 was found solely in the open phagosomal cup.
source: In stark contrast, PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 –which was visualized using AKT-PH-GFP– was found solely in the open phagosomal cup (Figure 6B), where it co-existed with PtdIns(3)P, detected using the PX-GFP sensor (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by AKT-PH-GFP biosensor data shown in Figure 6B

claim: PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 co-existed with PtdIns(3)P in the open phagosomal cup.
source: In stark contrast, PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 –which was visualized using AKT-PH-GFP– was found solely in the open phagosomal cup (Figure 6B), where it co-existed with PtdIns(3)P, detected using the PX-GFP sensor (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by biosensor data shown in Figure 6B and 6C

claim: Additional enrichment of PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 was detected in the actin cuff region (ratio cuff: cup 1.39 ± 0.10; n = 30, p=0.0006).
source: In addition to the localization of PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 in the cup reported in a previous collaborative study (Strijbis et al., 2013), we detected additional enrichment of PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 in the actin cuff region (ratio cuff: cup 1.39 ± 0.10; n = 30, p=0.0006).
evidence: Quantitative data from 30 measurements

claim: PtdIns(3)P was comparatively excluded from the actin cuff (ratio cuff: cup 0.823 ± 0.05; n = 30, p=0.0025).
source: In contrast, PtdIns(3)P was comparatively excluded from the actin cuff (ratio cuff: cup 0.823 ± 0.05; n = 30, p=0.0025).
evidence: Quantitative data from 30 measurements

claim: The segregation of phosphoinositides persisted for the duration of observations (up to 90 min after frustrated phagosome formation).
source: The segregation of these phosphoinositides persisted for the duration of our observations (up to 90 min after frustrated phagosome formation; not illustrated).
evidence: Observational data from time-lapse experiments

claim: LC3 was found in the frustrated phagosome yet did not reach the surface membrane.
source: As shown in Figure 6D, LC3 –a small protein covalently linked to PtdEth– was found in the frustrated phagosome (Kanayama and Shinohara, 2016; Martinez et al., 2015; Sprenkeler et al., 2016; Tam et al., 2016), yet did not reach the surface membrane.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Both wild-type Rab7 and constitutively-active Rab7 are confined to the frustrated phagosomal tube and partially excluded from the actin cuff.
source: Similarly, both wild-type Rab7 (Figure 6E) and constitutively-active Rab7 (not illustrated) are confined to the frustrated phagosomal tube and partially excluded from the actin cuff (Rab7 ratio cuff: cup 0.68 ± 0.05; n = 30, p<0.0001), as was LAMP1 (ratio cuff: cup 0.59 ± 0.03; n = 30, p<0.0001; Figure 6F), a late-endosomal/lysosomal membrane-spanning glycoprotein.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6E with quantification

claim: LAMP1 is confined to the frustrated phagosomal tube and partially excluded from the actin cuff (ratio cuff: cup 0.59 ± 0.03; n = 30, p<0.0001).
source: Similarly, both wild-type Rab7 (Figure 6E) and constitutively-active Rab7 (not illustrated) are confined to the frustrated phagosomal tube and partially excluded from the actin cuff (Rab7 ratio cuff: cup 0.68 ± 0.05; n = 30, p<0.0001), as was LAMP1 (ratio cuff: cup 0.59 ± 0.03; n = 30, p<0.0001; Figure 6F), a late-endosomal/lysosomal membrane-spanning glycoprotein.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6F with quantification

claim: Rapid recovery was observed following photobleaching of Rab7(Q67L) within the phagosomal cup, with half-maximal recovery attained after 3.3 s.
source: Rapid recovery was observed following photobleaching of a ≈3 µm spot within the phagosomal cup. In four independent experiments, half-maximal recovery was attained after 3.3 s (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 7B

claim: LAMP1-GFP recovered within seconds after photobleaching (t1/2 = 7.9 sec).
source: Similar analyses were performed using GFP-tagged LAMP1 (Figure 7A,B), which also recovered within seconds (t1/2 = 7.9 sec).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 7A and 7B

claim: Between 75–80% of the fluorescence was recovered for both Rab7(Q67L) and LAMP1, implying that the majority of these molecules were mobile.
source: Between 75–80% of the fluorescence was recovered in both instances, implying that the majority of the Rab7(Q67L) and LAMP1 molecules were mobile.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data analysis

claim: The fluorescence of the phagosomal cup containing Lyn11-GFP failed to recover after photobleaching, with only 19% of the original fluorescence reappearing.
source: Strikingly, the fluorescence of the cup failed to recover, despite the persistence of abundant Lyn11-GFP in the adjacent plasmalemma. In three independent experiments only 19% of the original fluorescence reappeared, possibly via fusion with Lyn11-GFP-containing early endosomes.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data from three independent experiments

claim: Lyn11-GFP displayed very fast and nearly complete recovery following photobleaching in the plasma membrane.
source: Failure to recover was not attributable to immobility of Lyn11-GFP in the membrane, which displayed very fast and nearly complete recovery following photobleaching (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 7D and 7E

claim: The region of the actin cuff acts as a lateral diffusion barrier, separating the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane from that of the open phagocytic cup.
source: These data confirm that the region of the actin cuff acts as a lateral diffusion barrier, separating the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane from that of the open phagocytic cup.
evidence: Inferred from the FRAP experiments with Lyn11-GFP

claim: Exofacial lipids and lipid-associated proteins readily traverse the junction between the membrane and the tubular phagosome.
source: It is noteworthy that while the barrier curtails the diffusion of lipids and proteins anchored to lipids on the inner leaflet of the membrane, exofacial lipids and lipid-associated proteins readily traverse the junction between the membrane and the tubular phagosome.
evidence: Inferred from the rhodamine-PtdEth and cholera toxin B labeling experiments

claim: Rhodamine-labeled PtdEth inserted into the outer leaflet of the plasmalemma reached the entire membrane of the frustrated phagocytic cup within approximately 5 min.
source: This was demonstrated by incorporation of rhodamine-labeled PtdEth to the surface membrane following stabilization of the frustrated phagosome. The labeled lipid, which inserts into the outer leaflet of the plasmalemma, reached the entire membrane of the frustrated phagocytic cup within ≈5 min (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: Fluorescent cholera toxin B subunit, which binds to exofacial ganglioside GM1, promptly entered the phagocytic cup.
source: Similarly, fluorescent cholera toxin B subunit, which binds to exofacial ganglioside GM1, promptly entered the phagocytic cup (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: The actin-dependent diffusion barrier selectively restricts the mobility of components of the inner leaflet, including transmembrane proteins, while exofacial lipids remain able to traverse the junction.
source: Thus, the actin-dependent diffusion barrier selectively restricted the mobility of components of the inner leaflet, including transmembrane proteins, while exofacial lipids remained able to traverse the junction.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental results on lipid and protein mobility

claim: CD2-CD45-GFP was largely (81%) and significantly (p>0.0001) excluded from CR3 patches after antibody-induced cross-linking.
source: After antibody treatment, CR3 clustered into large, dense patches. Strikingly, CD2-CD45-GFP was largely (81%) and significantly (p>0.0001) excluded from such patches, where the fluorescence was only 0.13 ± 0.01 of the plasmalemmal average (measured in 472 CR3 patches in 15 cells from three experiments).
evidence: Quantitative data from 472 CR3 patches in 15 cells from three experiments

claim: The exclusion of CD2-CD45-GFP from CR3 patches was not alleviated by treatment with latrunculin A.
source: Importantly, the exclusion was not alleviated by treatment with latrunculin A, the fluorescence of the patches averaging 0.12 ± 0.01 of the plasmalemmal average (measured in 445 patches in 18 cells from three experiments), implying that the actin cytoskeleton is not involved in the domain segregation.
evidence: Quantitative data from 445 patches in 18 cells from three experiments

claim: The actin cytoskeleton is not involved in the domain segregation caused by CR3 clustering.
source: Importantly, the exclusion was not alleviated by treatment with latrunculin A, the fluorescence of the patches averaging 0.12 ± 0.01 of the plasmalemmal average (measured in 445 patches in 18 cells from three experiments), implying that the actin cytoskeleton is not involved in the domain segregation.
evidence: Inferred from the latrunculin A treatment results

claim: Integrins can be sufficiently clustered to exclude other membrane components.
source: We concluded that integrins could be sufficiently clustered to exclude other membrane components.
evidence: Inferred from the CR3 patching experiments

claim: By forming a continuous and thick ring around the neck of the frustrated phagosome, the molecular crowding of clustered integrins could generate a diffusional barrier.
source: By forming a continuous and thick ring around the neck of the frustrated phagosome, the molecular crowding of clustered integrins could generate a diffusional barrier.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the CR3 clustering and exclusion data

claim: While antibody-induced clustering of CR3 was sufficient to form an actin-independent diffusional barrier, actin was required to maintain the barrier function of the cuff during phagocytosis of hyphae.
source: While antibody-induced clustering of CR3 was sufficient to form an actin-independent diffusional barrier, actin was required to maintain the barrier function of the cuff during phagocytosis of hyphae.
evidence: Inferred from the CR3 patching and latrunculin experiments

claim: Actin can stabilize integrins in their active conformation.
source: Actin can stabilize integrins in their active conformation (Kaizuka et al., 2007; Lavi et al., 2007; Lavi et al., 2012), and such stabilization is likely required to maintain the cuff during extended frustrated phagocytosis.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kaizuka et al., 2007; Lavi et al., 2007; Lavi et al., 2012

claim: PtdIns(4,5)P2 present in the cup, expressed relative to the plasmalemma, increased 4.88 times after latrunculin treatment.
source: PtdIns(4,5)P2 –which in untreated cells is excluded from the phagocytic cup (Figures 6A and 9A)– gained access to the entire cup when actin was disassembled by latrunculin (Figure 9B). The PtdIns(4,5)P2 present in the cup, expressed relative to the plasmalemma, increased 4.88 times after latrunculin treatment (Figure 9C).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 9C

claim: After latrunculin treatment, the ratio of LAMP1 present in the cup decreased 3.99 times.
source: Conversely, LAMP1 –that is restricted to the cup in untreated cells (Figures 6F and 9D)– was able to reach the surface membrane following treatment with latrunculin (Figure 9E). After latrunculin treatment, the ratio of LAMP1 present in the cup decreased 3.99 times (Figure 9F).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 9F

claim: While clustering of CR3 is sufficient to form a diffusional barrier, the actin cuff formed during phagocytosis of C. albicans hyphae likely contributes to the stability of the barrier.
source: Clearly, while clustering of CR3 is sufficient to form a diffusional barrier (Figure 8), the actin cuff formed during phagocytosis of C. albicans hyphae likely contributes to the stability of the barrier between CR3 and C. albicans β(1,3)-glucans, presumably by maintaining integrins in their active conformation (Kaizuka et al., 2007; Lavi et al., 2007; Lavi et al., 2012) during frustrated phagocytosis.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental results and supported by citations

claim: Frustrated phagosomes acquired markers of endosomes and lysosomes, implying that they had undergone at least partial maturation.
source: Despite remaining unsealed, frustrated phagosomes acquired markers of endosomes and lysosomes, implying that they had undergone at least partial maturation.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of LAMP1, Rab7, and LC3 in frustrated phagosomes

claim: LysoBrite Red dye never accumulated inside the frustrated phagosome.
source: We first tested the ability of frustrated phagosomes to generate and maintain an acidic lumen, using the fluorescent acidotropic dye LysoBrite Red dye. As expected, the dye accumulated in lysosomes; however, it was never found to concentrate inside the frustrated phagosome (Figure 10A), suggesting that vacuolar ATPases are not functional on its membrane and/or that the junction separating the lumen from the extracellular milieu is permeable to H+.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A

claim: The 10 kDa dextran was not detectable inside frustrated phagosomes.
source: The smaller (10 kDa) dextran, however, was not detectable inside frustrated phagosomes; the reduced overall staining of the cells (cf. main panel and inset in Figure 10B) suggests that secretion of lysosomes did occur, but that the dextran must have escaped the confines of the frustrated phagosome.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10B

claim: The 70 kDa dextran was readily visible along the frustrated phagosome, implying that its diffusion into the external medium was limited.
source: In contrast, the 70 kDa dextran was readily visible along the frustrated phagosome, implying that its diffusion into the external medium was limited.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10C

claim: A size-selective filter determines the extent to which solutes are retained within the frustrated phagosome.
source: Thus, a size-selective filter determined the extent to which solutes were retained within the frustrated phagosome.
evidence: Inferred from the differential retention of 10 kDa vs 70 kDa dextrans

claim: The cut-off of the size-selective filter must be greater than approximately 50 kDa.
source: The cut-off of this filter must be greater than ≈50 kDa, because cathepsin D, a globular protein of ≈28 kDa, managed to escape the frustrated phagosome (Figure 10D), yet was routinely detected in sealed phagosomes (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inferred from the cathepsin D data shown in Figure 10D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B

claim: The incomplete phagocytic cup formed around partially internalized hyphae would be expected to have limited degradative capacity towards C. albicans.
source: Therefore, the incomplete phagocytic cup formed around partially internalized hyphae would be expected to have limited degradative capacity towards C. albicans.
evidence: Inferred from the inability to retain small molecular weight hydrolases

claim: Formazan was preferentially deposited inside frustrated phagosomes, indicating superoxide production.
source: Indeed, we were able to detect preferential deposition of formazan, a product of the reaction of superoxide with nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT), inside frustrated phagosomes (Figure 10E).
evidence: Supported by NBT assay data shown in Figure 10E

claim: C. albicans hyphae grew at a rate of 0.22 µm min−1 ±0.03 in RPMI medium without serum (without macrophages present).
source: When measured in RPMI medium without serum (wthout macrophages present) C. albicans hyphae grew at a rate of 0.22 µm min−1 ±0.03.
evidence: Quantitative data from growth rate measurements

claim: The extension rate of partially internalized hyphae, which displayed an actin cuff, was significantly reduced (0.11 µm min−1 ±0.01).
source: Remarkably, the extension rate of partially internalized hyphae, which displayed an actin cuff, was significantly reduced (0.11 µm min−1 ±0.01).
evidence: Quantitative data from growth rate measurements shown in Figure 10F

claim: The reduced growth rate of partially internalized hyphae was not different (p=0.742) from that of fully internalized hyphae (0.108 µm min−1 ±0.011).
source: This reduced growth rate was not different (p=0.742) to that of fully internalized hyphae (0.108 µm min−1 ±0.011).
evidence: Quantitative data from growth rate measurements

claim: Neighboring C. albicans hyphae not in contact with macrophages grew at a rate of 0.198 µm min−1 ±0.014, indistinguishable from that measured in the absence of macrophages.
source: In the same experiments, neighboring C. albicans hyphae not in contact with macrophages grew at a rate of 0.198 µm min−1 ±0.014, indistinguishable from that measured in the absence of macrophages.
evidence: Quantitative data from growth rate measurements

claim: Small molecular weight contents are retained sufficiently in the frustrated phagosome to limit the growth of partially internalized C. albicans.
source: Therefore, while small molecular weight contents can eventually diffuse out of the frustrated phagosome, they are nevertheless retained sufficiently to limit the growth of partially internalized C. albicans.
evidence: Inferred from the growth rate data showing reduced extension of partially internalized hyphae

claim: The microbiostatic effect on partially internalized C. albicans hyphae could be ablated by blocking macrophage CR3 with the M1/70 antibody before phagocytosis.
source: This microbiostatic effect on partially internalized C. albicans hyphae could be ablated by blocking macrophage CR3 with the M1/70 antibody (see Figure 3F,G and H) before phagocytosis (Figure 10—figure supplement 2), reiterating the importance of CR3 ligation to β(1,3)-glucan for the generation and maintenance of this atypical phagocytic environment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2

claim: Macrophages generate de novo a strikingly effective diffusion barrier by a process that involves activation of integrins that induce the formation of a thick F-actin cuff at the neck of the tubular phagosomes.
source: Nevertheless, our study shows that macrophages endeavor to seal the frustrated phagocytic compartment, in an effort to maximize their antimicrobial effect and minimize the release of inflammatory agents. To this end, they generate de novo a strikingly effective diffusion barrier by a process that involves activation of integrins that induce the formation of a thick F-actin cuff at the neck of the tubular phagosomes.
evidence: Summary inference from the collective experimental results
